items.title: Critical Vulnerabilities Discovered in Google Chrome and Arm GPU Drivers
items.summary: Florian Schweitzer, Security Researcher at Certitude Consulting, has identified two serious vulnerabilities in products from Google and Arm that affect the same attack vector in the GPU software stack used by modern web browsers and mobile devices (CVE-2026-9034 and CVE-2026-93374). The issue can be triggered via JavaScript and could enable a sandbox escape. Such vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to compromise a user’s device after they visit a website. The discovery comes at a time of significant changes in vulnerability research, driven by the increasing use of artificial intelligence. The starting point for Schweitzer’s research was a deliberate decision not to compete with the enormous computing resources already being used to identify vulnerabilities in Chrome. “My strategy was simple: If you can’t compete with Google’s computing resources, you shouldn’t even try. I wanted to find attack surfaces that are difficult to integrate into a fuzzer or a fully automated AI workflow: real devices, stateful behavior, and boundaries between systems,” Schweitzer explained. Nevertheless, Schweitzer made extensive use of AI to generate WebGPU workloads, create automated test harnesses and device instrumentation, modify and compile Chromium, process crash data, and assist with reverse engineering the proprietary GPU driver. Rather than treating the model’s conclusions as definitive answers, he followed a process inspired by Austrian philosopher Karl Popper: formulating competing hypotheses, turning them into experiments, and attempting to falsify them as early and cost-effectively as possible. “The economics become interesting when the cost of failure decreases. If a hypothesis that would previously have taken several weeks to test can now be tested and discarded within a few hours, security researchers can conduct significantly more experiments. The competitive advantage increasingly lies in deciding which questions are worth asking, which evidence can be trusted, and which results warrant another hour of investigation,” said Marc Nimmerrichter, Managing Partner at Certitude Consulting. Critical Chrome Vulnerabilities Compared: 2025 and 2026 Certitude’s analysis of Google’s public Chrome Stable security releases shows that only four critical Chrome vulnerabilities were fixed in 2025. Three of these were reported by external security researchers, while one was attributed to Google. As of September 17, 2026, the same public data lists 179 critical vulnerabilities fixed in 2026: 145 attributed to Google and 34 to external researchers. External researchers have therefore already contributed more than ten times as many critical findings as in the previous year. At the same time, the number of critical findings attributed internally to Google has increased from one in 2025 to 145 in 2026. This shift coincides with Google’s rapid expansion of AI use in security research. In July, the Chrome Security Team described this as a “massive shift in the software security industry” and explained that large language models enable automated vulnerability discovery on a scale beyond traditional human research. Google states that it now uses AI throughout the entire vulnerability lifecycle, including vulnerability discovery, reproduction, triage, and remediation. The first vulnerability reported by Schweitzer, CVE-2026-9034, affects the Arm Mali GPU userspace driver. According to the public security advisory, an unprivileged process executing valid GPU operations “via WebGL or WebGPU” could access previously freed memory. The vulnerability affects several generations of Arm GPU drivers, including the 5th Gen GPU architecture, which provides graphics and compute capabilities for a wide range of consumer devices, including smartphones, tablets, TVs, and wearables. The second vulnerability, CVE-2026-93374, affects Google Chrome. Google classifies it as critical and describes it as a “use after free in Dawn,” Chromium’s implementation of WebGPU. The public CVE description identifies the issue as remotely exploitable via a crafted HTML page and as a potential sandbox escape: “Use after free in Dawn in Google Chrome on Android prior to 153.0.8010.52 allowed a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: Critical)” Potential Sandbox Escape The Chrome sandbox is a key security boundary designed to restrict access to the underlying operating system by exposed browser components responsible for rendering websites. Vulnerabilities that can bypass this boundary are therefore particularly dangerous. Exploit code can be delivered via a link to a website. Google credits Florian Schweitzer with reporting the Chrome vulnerability on April 8, 2026. Arm also publicly names Schweitzer of Certitude Consulting as the discoverer of CVE-2026-9034. Detailed technical information is intentionally being withheld during the coordinated disclosure process to avoid providing information that could enable exploitation before affected systems are adequately protected. Further details will be published at an appropriate time. Public References Arm Security Advisory: CVE-2026-9034, September 8, 2026 https://support.arm.com/documentation/111552/1-0/?lang=en NIST NVD: CVE-2026-9034 https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-9034 Google Chrome Security Announcement: CVE-2026-93374, September 17, 2026 https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2026/09/stable-channel-update-for-desktop_0194356994.html NIST NVD: CVE-2026-93374 https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-93374

Florian Schweitzer, Security Researcher at Certitude Consulting, has identified two serious vulnerabilities in products from Google and Arm that affect the same attack vector in the GPU software stack used by modern web browsers and mobile devices (CVE-2026-9034 and CVE-2026-93374). The issue can be triggered via JavaScript and could enable a sandbox escape. Such vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to compromise a user’s device after they visit a website.

The discovery comes at a time of significant changes in vulnerability research, driven by the increasing use of artificial intelligence.

The starting point for Schweitzer’s research was a deliberate decision not to compete with the enormous computing resources already being used to identify vulnerabilities in Chrome.

“My strategy was simple: If you can’t compete with Google’s computing resources, you shouldn’t even try. I wanted to find attack surfaces that are difficult to integrate into a fuzzer or a fully automated AI workflow: real devices, stateful behavior, and boundaries between systems,” Schweitzer explained.

Nevertheless, Schweitzer made extensive use of AI to generate WebGPU workloads, create automated test harnesses and device instrumentation, modify and compile Chromium, process crash data, and assist with reverse engineering the proprietary GPU driver. Rather than treating the model’s conclusions as definitive answers, he followed a process inspired by Austrian philosopher Karl Popper: formulating competing hypotheses, turning them into experiments, and attempting to falsify them as early and cost-effectively as possible.

“The economics become interesting when the cost of failure decreases. If a hypothesis that would previously have taken several weeks to test can now be tested and discarded within a few hours, security researchers can conduct significantly more experiments. The competitive advantage increasingly lies in deciding which questions are worth asking, which evidence can be trusted, and which results warrant another hour of investigation,” said Marc Nimmerrichter, Managing Partner at Certitude Consulting.

Critical Chrome Vulnerabilities Compared: 2025 and 2026

Certitude’s analysis of Google’s public Chrome Stable security releases shows that only four critical Chrome vulnerabilities were fixed in 2025. Three of these were reported by external security researchers, while one was attributed to Google.

As of September 17, 2026, the same public data lists 179 critical vulnerabilities fixed in 2026: 145 attributed to Google and 34 to external researchers. External researchers have therefore already contributed more than ten times as many critical findings as in the previous year. At the same time, the number of critical findings attributed internally to Google has increased from one in 2025 to 145 in 2026.

This shift coincides with Google’s rapid expansion of AI use in security research. In July, the Chrome Security Team described this as a “massive shift in the software security industry” and explained that large language models enable automated vulnerability discovery on a scale beyond traditional human research. Google states that it now uses AI throughout the entire vulnerability lifecycle, including vulnerability discovery, reproduction, triage, and remediation.

The first vulnerability reported by Schweitzer, CVE-2026-9034, affects the Arm Mali GPU userspace driver. According to the public security advisory, an unprivileged process executing valid GPU operations “via WebGL or WebGPU” could access previously freed memory. The vulnerability affects several generations of Arm GPU drivers, including the 5th Gen GPU architecture, which provides graphics and compute capabilities for a wide range of consumer devices, including smartphones, tablets, TVs, and wearables.

The second vulnerability, CVE-2026-93374, affects Google Chrome. Google classifies it as critical and describes it as a “use after free in Dawn,” Chromium’s implementation of WebGPU. The public CVE description identifies the issue as remotely exploitable via a crafted HTML page and as a potential sandbox escape: “Use after free in Dawn in Google Chrome on Android prior to 153.0.8010.52 allowed a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: Critical)”

Potential Sandbox Escape

The Chrome sandbox is a key security boundary designed to restrict access to the underlying operating system by exposed browser components responsible for rendering websites. Vulnerabilities that can bypass this boundary are therefore particularly dangerous. Exploit code can be delivered via a link to a website.

Google credits Florian Schweitzer with reporting the Chrome vulnerability on April 8, 2026. Arm also publicly names Schweitzer of Certitude Consulting as the discoverer of CVE-2026-9034.

Detailed technical information is intentionally being withheld during the coordinated disclosure process to avoid providing information that could enable exploitation before affected systems are adequately protected. Further details will be published at an appropriate time.

items.title: Microsoft Windows Shell 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: Microsoft has patched an actively exploited Windows Shell zero-day vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass Mark of the Web protections. Tracked as CVE-2026-96951, the flaw was addressed in the October 2026 Patch Tuesday updates . It carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and is rated Important by Microsoft. The vulnerability was not publicly disclosed before the update, but Microsoft confirmed that exploitation had already occurred. Its “Exploitation Detected” assessment signals a confirmed attack rather than a possible future threat. Microsoft’s Exploitability Index advises customers to give applicable updates in this category the highest priority. Windows Shell 0-Day Exploited The flaw involves command injection, where Windows Shell fails to properly handle special elements used in a command. Microsoft describes the outcome as a security feature bypass available to an unauthorized attacker over a network. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to evade Mark of the Web defenses. Mark of the Web identifies files that come from the internet and helps Windows apply warnings or other protective checks. Bypassing this protection can remove an important barrier between a downloaded file and a user opening dangerous content. However, the reported impact is a security bypass, not a standalone remote code execution flaw. Attackers can deliver a specially crafted file through email or instant messaging and use social engineering to persuade the target to open it. Exploitation requires user action. This means the flaw should not be treated as a zero-click attack, despite its network-based delivery path. Earlier reporting on Windows LNK Stomping attacks described another way attackers bypassed Mark of the Web through Windows shortcuts. Separately, a WinZip Mark of the Web vulnerability showed how archive extraction could lose internet-origin tags. These are separate vulnerabilities, not confirmed techniques used in the current attacks. The supplied Microsoft advisory credits Riku Bamba and Yuya Chudo of Fujitsu Limited, Benoit Sevens using Claude with Anthropic, and researcher yhw. It does not identify the attackers, their targets, the malicious file format, or the scale of exploitation. Those missing details limit conclusions about the campaign and its reach. Security teams should prioritize applicable Windows updates and check Microsoft’s Security Update Guide for affected products. Testing and deploying the fix quickly is especially important because exploitation is confirmed. Users should remain cautious with unexpected attachments, since this attack depends on persuading someone to interact with attacker-controlled content. An EDR alert reveals an attack. items.title: OpenAI Engineer Arrested for Planting Spyware Device in an Executive Conference Room
items.summary: An OpenAI engineer has been arrested for allegedly hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco offices. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, 2026, and appeared in federal court on October 13, according to the U.S. Department of Justice . Prosecutors charged him with using or attempting to use a device to intercept spoken communications. Although described as a spyware device in the headline, the hardware was a hidden audio recorder. The public announcement does not describe malware installed on OpenAI computers. OpenAI Engineer Arrested for Planting Spyware According to the complaint, OpenAI staff discovered the first device around September 30. It was plugged into a USB port behind a television, wrapped in toilet paper, and contained encrypted data. OpenAI determined that it had been installed around September 28. We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re… — OpenAI Newsroom (@OpenAINewsroom) October 13, 2026 The room hosted highly confidential discussions about research, product plans, business opportunities, government engagements, and technical progress. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan, who joined OpenAI in July 2025, had no authority to enter the room or attend those meetings. Office CCTV allegedly showed him near the room on several dates before the discovery. Footage from October 5 reportedly showed him entering the room and looking behind the television. Investigators also examined searches made through a productivity tool. Before September 28, Alfozan allegedly asked about building addresses, room calendars, meeting capacities, leadership locations, and meetings with outside partners. The complaint describes related prompts from a chatbot account associated with his spouse. Authorities said that account shared several identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s account. Between September 24 and September 30, it requested help with continuous audio recording, Wi-Fi connectivity, live listening, remote access, concealment, and SD card encryption. Prompts submitted on September 27 and September 28 allegedly referenced the first recorder’s custom header and unique MAC address. These details form part of the evidence linking the account activity to the recovered hardware. However, requests about remote access do not establish that recordings were transmitted outside OpenAI. On October 5, security staff also found a similar recorder inside a bag Alfozan allegedly left unattended elsewhere in the office. The bag contained his wallet and identification. The case concerns alleged physical eavesdropping, not a confirmed network breach. The Justice Department announcement does not identify a foreign recipient or establish that confidential recordings reached another party. Separately, Cybersecurity News has covered OpenAI’s response to AI reasoning extraction and researchers reaching internal repositories through a forum security flaw . Those reports concern different security paths and are not evidence of a connection to this case. The FBI is investigating. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Parker is prosecuting, with support from National Security Division attorney Kate Tagert. According to the Northern District of California announcement , Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release if convicted.
